summary:
Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023, establishes real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantees LGTBI rights. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own civil registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative self-identification route that replaced the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis plus two years of medical treatment. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, and the law regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16.

Other operative provisions of the same statute include a ban on non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children, expanded assisted reproduction rules, parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, strengthened sexuality education, and anti-discrimination measures covering healthcare, employment and housing. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force since 2005, and legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules in Spain, in contrast to the stricter single-sex-space approach being adopted in the United Kingdom on biological-sex lines with restrictions applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

There is no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime: the phrase 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510 (one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months) derive from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 itself reformed offences against sexual freedom, including Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravation is documented at first-instance level. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case concerning threats sent by WhatsApp to a trans woman, fining the author EUR 300. In a separate case reported on 8 January 2026, a juvenile gang harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park in Valencia to mock them; the only adult defendant received six months' prison and two minors were judged separately.

Comparatively, Spain's administrative self-declaration regime places it alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay. A 2016 23-country survey ranked Spain the most trans-supportive of the group surveyed and the only country where a majority supported unrestricted legal gender designation change, a dated baseline predating the 2023 law.
tangentialFactors:
Attitudes and safety vary geographically within Spain. Operator guidance rates the country as safe and welcoming for LGBTQIA+ travellers, especially in Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia, while noting that attitudes can be more conservative outside the big cities; the national tourism institute lists eight flagship LGBTQ+ destinations (Madrid's Chueca, Barcelona, Valencia, Seville, Cádiz, the Canary Islands, Sitges and Torremolinos) under a 'Destinations for Diversity' certification for discrimination-free spaces. A UK government travel advisory likewise describes Spain as a generally tolerant and progressive place for LGBT+ travellers with active communities and social venues, alongside standard crime warnings.

Official hostility has not disappeared. Under Franco's dictatorship from 1936 to 1975 thousands of gay men and women were jailed, held in camps or confined to mental institutions, some in prisons known as galerías de invertidos, and vagrancy laws were applied to suspected dissidents on the basis of actual or perceived homosexuality; trans people were prosecuted under public-scandal offences and municipal legislation until the end of the 1980s. In 2013 a serving Interior Minister publicly stated that same-sex marriage endangered the survival of the human species.

Contemporary backlash is regionally concentrated. After a regional election in 2023, the government of the Madrid region repealed that region's non-discrimination law, repealed the local conversion therapy ban insofar as it applies to trans people, removed penalties for conversion therapy and repealed several trans legal recognitions. National public opinion remains broadly accepting, with 88% acceptance recorded in a 2013 Pew poll, the highest of 39 countries surveyed.
localsOnly:
Residents use the same Civil Registry route as visitors for rectification of the gender mention, without a diagnosis or medical-treatment history, and minors aged 12 to 16 have regulated consent provisions for medical procedures under the same statute.

Anti-discrimination protection in healthcare, employment and housing is statutory, and the hate-speech aggravating circumstance of Article 22.4 plus Article 510 penalties of one to four years' imprisonment with a six to twelve-month fine apply to identity-motivated conduct. The aggravating circumstance for gender identity is being applied by trial courts in practice, as the Vigo misdemeanour sentence shows.

Regional law is not uniform: the Madrid region rolled back its own non-discrimination statute, conversion therapy penalties and several trans legal recognitions following the 2023 regional election, so protections that hold nationally can be weaker at regional level. Statistics on identity-motivated violence are contested between official and civil-society sources.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Madrid region's repeals of its conversion therapy ban and trans legal recognitions remain in force, or have been challenged or reinstated, is not resolved by the sources here; the inventory records the 2023 repeals only.

Violence figures conflict and are not reconciled: the Secretary of State for Security reported a 4% decrease in 2018, the Observatorio Madrileño a 7% increase, and Catalonia's Observatori contra l'Homofòbia a 30% increase in early 2019. No consolidated national figure for gender-identity-motivated offences is sourced.

Only two enforcement outcomes are documented, both at first-instance or juvenile level; the frequency with which courts outside Vigo and Valencia apply the gender-identity aggravation is not sourced. Whether the 2016 attitude survey findings still hold after the 2023 law is unresolved, and no post-2023 polling of Spanish public opinion on trans legal recognition appears in the inventory.
